Additional stress will be sharply felt if significant coal mining other than Westmoreland is realized (Alternative Future 2). By the year 2000, large expansions of the water and sewer systems would have to be made, costing close to $5.5 million. Approximately half of the expansion would be needed by 1978 in order to accommodate large construction crews for Westmoreland and other mining operations. A delay in other mining development would reduce initial demands, although eventually they would be felt. The major concern is the speed at which these changes will occur and the ability of the city to obtain sufficient financial and technical aid to meet the immediate problems posed by such a situation. In 1986-89, out-migration is projected, reducing by 10 percent the demand for services and facilities. This presents a twin quandary: a lag in needed services followed by a temporary surplus capacity.
Although Hardin has and will continue to experience an increase in demand for services, the town receives little additional revenue from the coal. The coal property is not within city limits and is not subject to taxation by the city. Although incoming workers may spend a portion of their income in Hardin, there is no sales tax. The only additional revenue to the city is through property tax on new, rented and purchased residential units, and through funds made available from Coal Severance Tax revenues.
